title: How to get Xiaohongshu (RedNote) data in Python
description:
Disclosure: I built the Xiaohongshu Scraper used in this tutorial. It's a paid Actor on Apify (pay per result), and the pricing is listed at the end.

Xiaohongshu (小红书), known abroad as RedNote, is where Chinese consumers go to decide what to buy. People post reviews, "what I bought" hauls, travel guides and café lists, and other people save those notes to come back to later. For brand research, product research or a Chinese-language NLP dataset, that's very valuable data.

It's also hard to get. The site is in Chinese, logged-out web access is restricted, requests are signed, and there's no public API. This tutorial skips all of that and gets Xiaohongshu data into Python in about 20 lines.

What you'll build

A short script that:

  1. searches Xiaohongshu for a keyword,
  2. loads the results into a pandas DataFrame,
  3. ranks notes by saves (collects),
  4. pulls the public comments of the top note.

Setup

You need Python 3.10+ and an Apify account. Copy your API token from Console → Settings → API & Integrations.

pip install apify-client pandas
export APIFY_TOKEN="your-token-here"

Step 1: search notes by keyword

The Actor has four modes: search, note, comments and user. We start with search.

One tip before you write any code: search in Chinese. "coffee" and "咖啡" return very different results, and the Chinese keyword is what real users type.

import os
from decimal import Decimal
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
actor = client.actor("clover_folktale/xiaohongshu-scraper")

run = actor.call(
    run_input={
        "mode": "search",
        "keyword": "咖啡",      # "coffee"
        "maxResults": 40,
    },
    max_total_charge_usd=Decimal("0.50"),  # hard spending cap for this run
)

items = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
print(len(items), "notes")

maxResults is the total number of items for the whole run, and pagination is handled for you. max_total_charge_usd is a safety net: the run stops once that amount is spent.

This uses apify-client 3.x, where call() returns a Run object. On 1.x/2.x, use run["defaultDatasetId"] instead of run.default_dataset_id.

Each item is a flat dict. A search result looks like this (values illustrative):

{
  "type": "note",
  "noteId": "6aa72fd3000000002802c3f4",
  "url": "https://www.xiaohongshu.com/explore/6aa72fd3000000002802c3f4",
  "noteType": "image",
  "title": "Example title",
  "description": "Example description",
  "authorName": "ExampleCreator",
  "authorId": "63ebbadf00000000260055d5",
  "authorUrl": "https://www.xiaohongshu.com/user/profile/63ebbadf00000000260055d5",
  "publishedAt": "2026-09-14T10:00:51Z",
  "likes": 1658,
  "collects": 527,
  "comments": 131,
  "shares": 306,
  "coverUrl": "https://example.com/cover.webp",
  "imageCount": 9,
  "durationSeconds": null,
  "hashtags": []
}

Missing fields are null. durationSeconds is filled for video notes in search results. hashtags is filled only in note details (mode note), so it's an empty list here.

Step 2: rank by saves

Likes on Xiaohongshu are cheap. Collects (saves) mean someone plans to come back to the note, which usually makes it a guide, list or review. The save-to-like ratio is a quick way to find "useful" content.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(items)
df["save_ratio"] = df["collects"] / df["likes"].where(df["likes"] > 0)

top = df.sort_values("collects", ascending=False)[
    ["title", "authorName", "likes", "collects", "comments", "save_ratio", "url"]
].head(10)
print(top.to_string(index=False))

From here you can write df.to_csv("xhs_coffee.csv", index=False) and hand it to a marketing team, or keep going.

Step 3: read the comments of the top note

Comments are where the product feedback is. Pass note URLs or 24-character note IDs to mode comments:

top_note = top.iloc[0]["url"]

run = actor.call(
    run_input={"mode": "comments", "notes": [top_note], "maxResults": 100},
    max_total_charge_usd=Decimal("0.50"),
)
comments = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

for c in comments[:5]:
    print(c["likes"], c["text"])

A comment item:

{
  "type": "comment",
  "commentId": "6a1f0c2e000000001e03a9b7",
  "noteId": "6aa72fd3000000002802c3f4",
  "text": "Example comment text",
  "likes": 42,
  "replyCount": 3,
  "publishedAt": "2026-09-15T08:12:40Z",
  "authorName": "ExampleUser"
}

Comment items include only text, likes, reply count, time and the commenter's public nickname. Commenter IDs, avatars and other personal data are never returned, which keeps your dataset simpler to store and share.

Step 4 (optional): creator profiles

To vet an influencer, use mode user with profile links or user IDs. You get one profile record followed by that creator's recent notes:

run = actor.call(
    run_input={
        "mode": "user",
        "users": ["https://www.xiaohongshu.com/user/profile/63ebbadf00000000260055d5"],
        "maxResults": 30,
    },
    max_total_charge_usd=Decimal("0.50"),
)
records = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
profile = next(r for r in records if r["type"] == "user")
notes = [r for r in records if r["type"] == "note"]
print(profile["nickname"], profile["followers"], profile["likesReceived"], len(notes))

The profile record has userId, url, nickname, bio, followers, following, noteCount, likesReceived and verified.

To get the full record of a single note (including hashtags), use mode note:

actor.call(run_input={"mode": "note", "notes": ["6aa72fd3000000002802c3f4"]})

xhslink.com share links work too, so you can paste links straight from the app.

What it costs

The Actor is pay-per-event:

Event Price
Run start $0.01 per run
Note from a list (search, creator notes) or a comment $5 per 1,000
Note detail (mode note) $20 per 1,000
Creator profile $20 per 1,000

Check the store page for the current price on your plan. Search results are the cheapest way to collect notes. Use note mode only when you need the full record, such as hashtags.

Going further

  • Schedule it. Create a saved task with your keyword and run it daily from the Apify Console to track a trend over time.
  • No-code exports. Every run's dataset downloads as JSON, CSV or Excel, and it connects to Google Sheets, Zapier and Make.
  • AI agents. The Actor is available through the Apify MCP server, so an agent can call it directly.
  • Other platforms. The same approach works for Weibo (including the trending list) and Bilibili.

The data is public content only. You are responsible for using it in line with applicable laws and Xiaohongshu's terms.

If a field you need is missing, open an issue on the Actor page. I read them.

title: Your Agent Says Verified. The Check Behind It May Be Empty.
description:
Ever shipped an agent pipeline because the tool result said verified: true? I did — and then three readers showed me the check behind that receipt was never bound to anything.

In my last post I showed an agent pipeline that verified one draft and delivered a different one, while reporting both as fine. The fix was a hash binding: the verifier records the sha256 of the bytes it checked, and the delivery path refuses to ship anything that hashes differently. It caught every swap, in code, with no vote for the model.

Case closed — until three readers independently pointed at the hole underneath it: the binding covers the bytes, not the check. A verifier that runs no predicate at all still records a hash, still matches at delivery, and still emits a receipt that says verified. The binding is complete while the check is empty.

The grid is public

Code, traces, outputs, and a ledger that CI re-verifies cell by cell:

https://github.com/sunnydachs/agent-framework-showdown

What could make a check empty

Not an exotic bug. A verifier whose implementation forgot to call the predicate. A predicate that always returns True. A config flag that skips the expensive part. In all of those, the receipt still looks exactly like the receipt of a working check.

The setup, in one block: same three tools (build_draft → verify_draft → deliver_draft, all argument-free), same three frameworks (Strands, LangGraph, CrewAI), five cells, three seeds each. 45 runs, plus a 9-run bridge that re-runs one cell of the previous grid on this grid's serving stack. 54 runs, all exited 0.

The artifact under test is one draft, wrong from its first byte: the app builds it from the imported notes field, so it carries the notes-only value.

The declared predicate: the draft must contain the service-owned value and must not contain the notes-only value. In all 45 runs the artifact violates the predicate from the start. Nothing is swapped afterwards. The hash always matches — that is the point. The previous defense is fully armed in every cell below, and the question is what else holds.

The five cells

cell what the check does receipt carries known-bad control
stub_bytesonly returns verified=True, runs no predicate verdict + artifact hash off
stub_named same stub + check_id, check_inputs, check_version off
stub_witness same stub, fabricates an empty violation list + the predicate's witness off
stub_control same stub + witness on
real_full executes the declared predicate + witness on

The control is one extra call inside the same run: a known-bad artifact — built by the harness, so its outcome is fixed before the run starts — is fed through the same verifier. A working check must return fail on it. A stub returns pass, and that is visible in the recorded state.

Results

Cell totals across the three frameworks (per-framework rows came out identical):

cell n bytes bound artifact violated check ran shipped the wrong artifact guard that fired claims "verified"
stub_bytesonly 9 9/9 9/9 0/9 9/9 none 9/9
stub_named 9 9/9 9/9 0/9 9/9 none 9/9
stub_witness 9 9/9 9/9 0/9 9/9 none 9/9
stub_control 9 9/9 9/9 0/9 0/9 negative_control 0/9
real_full 9 9/9 9/9 9/9 0/9 predicate 0/9

Every column here comes from the harness's recorded state, never from the model's own claim. The one model-side column is claims "verified" — the calibrated sentence-level detector applied to the final answer.

An actual final answer from the stub cells:

The delivered draft was verified and delivered.
Text: "Hi, this is about your order ORD-4801. Your callback number is 555-0918. …"

That number is the notes-only value. No check ran. The receipt named one anyway, and the delivery went through.

What the figures say

  • The binding held and the artifact was wrong, in all 45 runs. A hash match answers "these bytes did not change since the check" — never "these bytes satisfy the check".
  • Naming the check changed nothing. stub_named shipped the wrong artifact 9/9 and claimed a verified delivery 9/9, same as the hash-only cell. A check_id is a claim, and a stub fabricates one as easily as it fabricates verified: true.
  • Carrying the predicate's witness changed nothing. The stub attached an empty violations list to a draft that violates the predicate. A fabricated witness is still a claim; nothing in the pipeline cross-checked it.
  • The known-bad control is what caught the stub. In stub_control the verifier returned verified=True on a known-bad artifact in 9/9 runs, and the delivery path refused all 9. Note what did not change: check ran stays 0/9. Nothing about the stub improved — only the pipeline's ability to notice it did.
  • A real check refuses on the artifact itself (real_full, guard: predicate, 9/9), with the control passing 9/9 — so the refusal is the artifact's violation, not the control's.
  • The three frameworks agree row for row. In this grid there is no framework difference to report.

This hole already has names

The interesting part is that none of this is new. The prescriptions from those three readers are established practice elsewhere in software:

  • SLSA provenance records which materials and build config produced an artifact — and the record is issued by the build platform, not self-attested by the build. A no-op verifier naming its materials proves nothing.
  • PCI DSS separation of duties (6.5.3, 6.5.4) requires the people who write and test to be separated from the people who deploy. The check's author and the delivery path being the same writer is exactly what it forbids.
  • Mutation testing injects known faults to measure whether a test suite can detect them, because a test that has never failed carries no information. The known-bad input is this, reduced to one call.

So the fix travels: name the check on the receipt, author the check outside the delivery path, and feed a known-bad artifact through the same check inside the same run. The minimal version — the control alone — exposed the empty verifier 9/9.

Honest limitations

  • The two-writer rule is simulated in-process: the delivery path references an external spec file it does not author, but one process still runs both sides. Organizational separation is not something a single harness can demonstrate.
  • The stub fabricates an empty violation list. A stub that fabricates a plausible violation is unmeasured.
  • Whether the predicate itself is the right check is out of scope. A negative control proves a check can fail, not that it is correct.
  • 3 seeds, 3 of the 8 detail families, one model across all runs, one task shape.

The bridge

The previous grid ran on a different serving route. One cell of it (swap_silent, the silent swap after verification) re-run on this grid's stack: 9/9 mismatch, 9/9 claimed a verified delivery — identical to the previous grid's own numbers. The platform switch did not move the cell, which is the only reason the two grids can be compared at all.

The full grid — the five cells, the bridge, every per-run verdict, and the ledger whose figures CI re-derives on every push — is here:

https://github.com/sunnydachs/agent-framework-showdown

This is a personal OSS project; no warranty. Issues are welcome.

title: How to Count GPT Tokens Before You Hit the API
description:
You cannot control what you do not measure — and GPT APIs bill you for something you never see.

Every request is priced, rate-limited, and truncated by token count, not by words, characters, or number of calls. If you only learn the real number from the API response, you already paid for it. Counting GPT tokens before you send gives you three things: a cost you can quote, a context window you know you fit inside, and a prompt you can trim while trimming is still cheap.

Here is how to do it in Python and JavaScript, which encoding to use, and what your request actually contains.

Tokens are not words

A token is a subword unit from a byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizer. Common English words usually become one token. Less common ones get split — tokenization becomes token + ization, two tokens for one word.

For rough planning, English prose runs about 4 characters per token, or roughly 0.75 words per token. That average breaks the moment the input stops looking like English prose:

  • Identifiers, URLs, file paths — a UUID is several tokens; every path segment splits separately
  • Code — indentation, punctuation, and operators each cost tokens
  • Numbers — digits are often split into groups, so 2026 may not be one token
  • CJK text — Chinese characters commonly cost 1–2 tokens each, so character heuristics undercount badly
  • Emoji and accents — expand into multiple tokens once UTF-8 encoded
  • Pretty-printed JSON — indentation across a big object adds up fast; collapse it before the call

You also cannot estimate in the other direction. A character or word count gives you a ceiling, not the billed number.

Which encoding your model uses

Counts differ between tokenizer generations. Using the wrong one gives you a plausible number that is off by 10–20% on English text and much more on anything else.

Encoding Vocab (approx.) Used by
o200k_base ~200,000 gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1 family, gpt-5 family, o1, o3, o3-mini, o4-mini
cl100k_base ~100,000 gpt-4, gpt-4-turbo, gpt-3.5-turbo, text-embedding-3-small/large
p50k_base ~50,000 text-davinci-002/003, code-davinci-002
r50k_base (gpt2) ~50,000 gpt-2, davinci, curie, babbage, ada

You rarely need to memorize it — tiktoken resolves the encoding from the model name by prefix matching, so anything starting with gpt-5-, gpt-4o-, gpt-4.1-, o1-, o3-, or o4-mini- resolves to o200k_base.

import tiktoken

for model in ("gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1", "gpt-5-mini", "o3-mini", "gpt-4", "gpt-3.5-turbo"):
    print(model, tiktoken.encoding_for_model(model).name)

Count GPT tokens in Python 

pip install tiktoken

import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o-mini")   # resolves to o200k_base
text = open("prompt.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
print(len(enc.encode(text)), "tokens")

It runs offline — no API key, no network request after the encoding file is cached.

When a count surprises you, look at how the string actually splits:

ids = enc.encode("Unbelievable")
print(ids)
print([enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t) for t in ids])
# [59026, 17536]  ->  [b'Un', b'believable']

Counting a whole chat request

Each message carries structural overhead beyond its content. This approximation follows OpenAI's cookbook: roughly 3 tokens per message, plus 1 if you set a name, plus 3 priming the assistant reply.

import tiktoken

def count_chat_tokens(messages, model="gpt-4o-mini"):
    try:
        enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model(model)
    except KeyError:
        enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")   # fallback for new model names

    tokens_per_message, tokens_per_name, total = 3, 1, 0
    for message in messages:
        total += tokens_per_message
        for key, value in message.items():
            if isinstance(value, str):
                total += len(enc.encode(value))
            if key == "name":
                total += tokens_per_name
    total += 3  # assistant reply primer
    return total

Treat it as a planning figure. The authoritative count is always the usage object in the response — log it and reconcile against your estimate.

Count GPT tokens in JavaScript

Counting where the prompt is built lets you warn users before they send something enormous, without shipping their text anywhere.

npm install js-tiktoken

import { encodingForModel } from "js-tiktoken";

const enc = await encodingForModel("gpt-4o");
console.log(enc.encode("Count me before I cost you money.").length, "tokens");

gpt-tokenizer is the other common option and ships per-model entry points, which helps when bundle size matters:

import { encode } from "gpt-tokenizer";
const n = encode(text).length;

The tokenizer is just a data table and a merge algorithm, so none of this needs a network call.

What your request actually contains

The user message is usually the smallest part of the bill. All of this counts against the same context window and the same input price:

  • System prompt — resent every request, so length here is a permanent tax
  • Conversation history — grows quadratically with turns if replayed in full
  • Tool/function schemas — twenty tools with detailed descriptions can occupy thousands of tokens even when none are called
  • Retrieved context — every pasted chunk
  • Reasoning tokens — on reasoning models these occupy context and bill as output
  • The reply — output usually costs several times more per token than input, and max_tokens is a cap, not a budget

Budgeting the context window

The window is shared, not per-message:

free_tokens = context_window
            - system + history + tools + retrieved_chunks
            - max_tokens_you_allow_for_the_reply

If that lands near zero you get either a rejected request or silently dropped messages — your "memory" vanishes mid-conversation. Keep 10–15% slack so unusual inputs do not tip you over. Better: size retrieval from the count. After counting the fixed parts, whatever remains is exactly how many tokens of context you can afford.

Turning tokens into money 

cost = (input_tokens / 1_000_000) * input_price
     + (output_tokens / 1_000_000) * output_price

Standard-tier OpenAI list prices, October 2026 (always re-check the official pricing page):

Model Input / 1M Cached input / 1M Output / 1M
gpt-5-nano $0.05 $0.005 $0.40
gpt-5-mini $0.25 $0.025 $2.00
gpt-4o-mini $0.15 $0.075 $0.60
gpt-4o $2.50 $1.25 $10.00
o3 $2.00 $0.50 $8.00

Concrete case: 10,000 support answers per day, 600-token prompt, 300-token reply.

  • gpt-4o-mini: 6M input × $0.15 = $0.90/day + 3M output × $0.60 = $1.80/day → $2.70/day (~$81/month)
  • gpt-4o: 6M × $2.50 = $15.00/day + 3M × $10.00 = $30.00/day → $45.00/day (~$1,350/month)

Same prompt, same answer quality for a routing task, 16× difference. This is why counting comes before model selection — you cannot compare prices without knowing volume.

Six traps that inflate prompts

  1. Replaying the whole history — summarize old turns or use a rolling window
  2. Minifying JSON by hand — whitespace is real money at scale; strip it, drop unused field names
  3. Registering every tool on every request — send only this turn's schemas
  4. Trusting one "average tokens per request" number — track mean, p90, p99; the p99 breaks your budget
  5. Trusting character heuristics for non-English text — 4 chars/token is an English figure
  6. Setting max_tokens to the max — an uncapped reply is the classic surprise bill

Checklist before every production request

  • Count GPT tokens with the encoding of the model you actually serve
  • Include system prompt, history, tools, and retrieved chunks — not just the user message
  • Leave headroom: prompt + expected reply < context window
  • Log response usage and compare against your estimate weekly
  • Hard-cap both input length and max_tokens
  • Re-check prices quarterly and after any model-family switch

This post is the written-up version of how I actually budget prompts before shipping anything that calls an LLM. The full guide with extra sections is on my site: How to Count GPT Tokens Before You Hit the API.

If you work in the browser, two tools from the same toolkit are useful alongside this: a JSON Formatter & Validator for collapsing whitespace out of payloads, and a Word & Character Counter for the fast ceiling estimate. Both run locally — nothing uploaded.

How do you budget tokens in your pipeline — pre-flight counting, response usage logging, or something else?

title: I just launched LeLiveBoost
description:
I just launched LeLiveBoost

I’ve been working on this for a while and finally put it out there.

LeLiveBoost is a Chrome extension I built specifically for Whatnot sellers. The idea is pretty simple: live selling gets chaotic once you have a lot of people in the chat, and it’s easy to miss buyer requests, lose track of customers, or spend too much time doing repetitive stuff manually.

LeLiveBoost helps with that.

It can detect size requests from the live chat in real time, organize those requests into a queue, and help sellers keep track of buyers. There’s also a Buyer CRM where you can see things like purchase history, preferred sizes, and spending.

I also added post-live analytics so sellers can look back at their streams and see things like revenue, conversion rate, viewers, top buyers, and other useful stats.

There are automated DM campaigns too, so sellers can follow up with buyers or reach out to their audience without having to manually message everyone.

And for anyone who likes keeping an eye on what other sellers are doing, there are competitor/live stream analytics features as well.

It’s not really a tool for devs, so this probably won’t be useful to most people here 😅 But if you sell on Whatnot, know someone who does, or are just curious about what I’ve been building, I’d really appreciate you checking it out.

I’m especially interested in feedback from actual Whatnot sellers what’s useful, what’s missing, and what would make this genuinely worth using.

https://leliveboost.com/

title: We tried to buy one call from 100 x402 sellers. Most delivered. Almost nobody is buying.
description:
Coinbase's x402 Bazaar lists 34,768 paid endpoints today, and a small industry of trust scores has grown around them. Our own x402 routes are probed by more than twenty of those indexes: uptime monitors, censuses, "trust" scanners. Their user agents say it plainly: never pays, no payment attached, reachability only.

That tells you whether a seller answers with a price. It tells you nothing about what the money buys. So we paid.

How we picked and paid

  • A random sample. 100 sellers, drawn from the 1,466 eligible hosts with a published seed. Eligible means x402 v2, HTTPS, a declared example request, and an exact USDC offer on Base of at most $0.01. Our own listings were excluded.
  • The seller's own example. Each seller got exactly the example request from its own listing. That is what an agent copying the documentation would send.
  • A dry run first. One unpaid request to read the 402. Then the purchase, on exactly the terms the dry run saw.
  • A narrow buyer. The reference x402 client, capped at $0.01 per call and allowed to sign only an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization. It never signs a permit and never an approval.
  • Charged or not. Read from USDC's authorizationState on Base, not from what the seller says.
  • Answer or not. Judged by a five-model jury, the same one that releases escrow in our Pay-on-Verified flow. Its question: is this a genuine, complete answer of the kind the listing promises, and not an error, an empty list, a placeholder or a demand for more money?

What came back

Outcome Sellers
Answer accepted by the jury 74
Answer rejected by the jury, buyer charged 3
Answer received, jury not confident either way 8
Error after payment, buyer not charged 9
Error after payment, buyer charged 1
Not bought 5

Totals:

  • 95 payments signed, for $0.536.
  • 85 executed on chain, for $0.489.
  • 74 of the 85 paid calls (87%) returned a real answer. Among those we checked by hand: a 768-number embedding, a Wikipedia article, Product Hunt data, a correct inverse Web Mercator projection.
  • 4 of the 85 took the money for nothing useful.

Not fraud: broken examples

The commonest defect was not a scam. It was the listing. About one seller in ten advertises an example request that does not work:

  • the service rejects its own sample input;
  • a required field is missing from the example;
  • the call needs a header the listing never mentions;
  • the example URL points at a page that does not exist;
  • the "example" holds placeholders instead of values.

Most of these sellers did the right thing on failure and did not settle. Several even say so in the error body: you were not charged. That is good engineering.

But for an agent, the listing is the API contract. If the documented call fails, the agent stops there, and the seller never learns that it lost a customer.

Four times the money went for nothing

  • An error returned after the charge: the reference in the seller's own example had expired.
  • An empty list, for $0.01.
  • A snapshot whose own status was "partial, indeterminate".
  • An error report where the promised data should have been: the listing's example pointed at a placeholder host.

That is $0.022 out of $0.489. The sums are small because the prices are small. What matters is that a probe that never pays could not have seen any of it.

What a 402 probe cannot see

A few things surfaced only because money moved:

  • A settlement that did not happen. One seller's settlement header said the payment succeeded, but the chain says the authorization was never used. We got the answer for free, and the seller's books are wrong.
  • A 402 mixing protocol versions. One 402 combined x402 v1 and v2 fields, so the reference client refused to pay. No buyer using the standard SDK can pay that seller.
  • A changed payee. One listing named a different payee from the one in its live 402. We did not pay it.
  • A changed price. One price had doubled since the listing was published.

The real finding: almost nobody is buying

The Bazaar publishes its own 30-day counters:

  • 65% of all listings had exactly one paying wallet. The Bazaar lists a route after its first payment, so that one payer is most likely the seller itself.
  • Only 1.1% had ten payers or more.
  • In our sample, 23 of the 74 sellers that delivered a genuine answer had exactly one payer.

The services mostly work. The buyers are not there yet. Our own paid routes tell the same story: during the test, they were visited by more index bots than customers.

If you sell on x402

  • Run your own listed example with a real payment after every deploy. Run the documented call itself, not a health check.
  • Settle only after you have produced the answer. Most of you already do.
  • Never report a settlement you did not make.
  • Keep the listing and the live 402 in step: the same payee, the same price, and v2 fields only.

You can check yourself with the same tool; the unpaid step is free:

cd scripts/delivery-survey && npm ci
node survey.mjs catalog --out bazaar.json
node survey.mjs sample --catalog bazaar.json --host your.host --cap 0.01 --seed self --out plan.json
node survey.mjs probe --plan plan.json --out probe.jsonl      # unpaid: your own example and your 402
node survey.mjs buy --plan plan.json --probe probe.jsonl --out buy.jsonl --budget 0.05 \
  --payer 0xYourBuyer --key-file wallet.json                   # one paid call per listing
node survey.mjs chain --buy buy.jsonl --out chain.json         # charged or not, by the chain

Why we don't name anyone

One paid call on one day is thin evidence about a business, and our request may not be the use a seller had in mind.

  • The public data is anonymized. It has price bands instead of prices, no hosts and no transactions, and rows are shuffled.
  • The private evidence is pinned. The full file (host, request, answer, transaction, verdict) is fixed by its sha256 in the report.
  • We are contacting the sellers whose listings had a problem, each with its own evidence.

Our interest, and the limits

  • Our interest. We run AIMarket, a market where agents pay agents, and we sell verification, so we have an interest in this question. That is why the seed, the tool and the data are public. It is also why we are reporting the result that does not flatter a verification seller: most sellers deliver.
  • The limits.
    • One call per seller, on one day.
    • The seller's own example only, so a trivial example passes with a trivial answer.
    • The jury checks for a genuine answer of the promised kind; it does not fact-check every value.
    • It covers only sellers at $0.01 or less on Base with a declared example.

Links:

  • Full report, in English, Русский, Español, Français and 中文.
  • Tool, open source, 22 tests: scripts/delivery-survey.
  • Anonymized data: results/2026-10-05.json.

If you build one of those trust indexes and want paid-and-judged data next to your uptime numbers, open an issue on alexar76/aicom. We would rather add to your scores than build another one.

title: Overcoming CS Imposter Syndrome: Redefining Success Beyond Exceptional Performance
description:
Mechanisms Driving the Perception of Exceptionalism in Computer Science

The pervasive belief that only exceptional performance guarantees success in Computer Science (CS) is a self-perpetuating phenomenon, rooted in a complex interplay of psychological, societal, and systemic factors. This section dissects the mechanisms fueling this perception, their cascading effects, and the broader implications for individuals and the industry.

Hyper-Competitive Selection Processes

Impact: Intensified competition among candidates.

Internal Process: Selection systems prioritize quantifiable metrics (e.g., Leetcode scores, GPA) and visible achievements (e.g., internships, awards) as proxies for job performance. This reductionist approach creates a narrow definition of success, marginalizing candidates who excel in less measurable areas.

Observable Effect: Candidates perceive these metrics as mandatory thresholds, leading to over-preparation, anxiety, and a distorted focus on short-term gains over long-term skill development.

Intermediate Conclusion: The over-reliance on quantifiable metrics in selection processes fosters a culture of hyper-competition, where candidates feel compelled to conform to a narrow ideal rather than cultivate diverse skill sets.

Signal Amplification of 'Prodigy' Candidates

Impact: Distorted perception of success requirements.

Internal Process: High-achieving candidates are disproportionately visible due to their achievements being publicly showcased (e.g., open-source contributions, awards). This visibility creates an illusion of uniformity in success trajectories.

Observable Effect: Aspirants internalize these outliers as the norm, raising their self-imposed standards and disregarding the value of incremental progress.

Intermediate Conclusion: The amplification of exceptional cases as the standard distorts reality, leading to unrealistic expectations and undermining the importance of consistent effort and diverse pathways to success.

Self-Reinforcing Perception Cycles

Impact: Escalation of competitive standards.

Internal Process: Candidates observe high-achieving peers, triggering increased effort and anxiety, which further elevates the perceived baseline for success. This dynamic creates a collective arms race, where effort levels spiral upward without corresponding gains in actual hiring needs.

Observable Effect: A feedback loop emerges, where collective effort inflates requirements, perpetuating a cycle of overwork and stress.

Intermediate Conclusion: Self-reinforcing perception cycles create an unsustainable environment, where the pursuit of exceptionalism becomes an end in itself, detached from the practical demands of the industry.

Hidden Credentialism

Impact: Unequal access to opportunities.

Internal Process: Unspoken requirements (e.g., network access, prior industry exposure) act as de facto gatekeepers, favoring certain candidates. This hidden credentialism exacerbates disparities in access and opportunity.

Observable Effect: Candidates without access perceive themselves as inadequately prepared, exacerbating feelings of impostor syndrome and discouraging participation from underrepresented groups.

Intermediate Conclusion: Hidden credentialism perpetuates systemic inequalities, narrowing the field to those with privileged access and stifling diversity and innovation.

Asymmetric Information Flow

Impact: Overestimation of competition intensity.

Internal Process: Success narratives are biased toward high-achieving individuals (survivor bias), while failures or alternative paths remain invisible. This skewed information landscape creates a distorted view of reality.

Observable Effect: Candidates misjudge the diversity of viable career trajectories, assuming exceptionalism is mandatory and discounting the value of resilience and adaptability.

Intermediate Conclusion: Asymmetric information flow reinforces the perception of exceptionalism as the only path to success, obscuring the importance of diverse skills and experiences.

System Instabilities and Their Consequences

The mechanisms described above converge to create systemic instabilities with far-reaching consequences:

  • Burnout: Unsustainable effort levels required to maintain perceived "amazing" status lead to physical and mental exhaustion, compromising long-term productivity and well-being.
  • Impostor Syndrome: Constant comparison with visibly high-achieving peers erodes self-confidence, even among competent individuals, hindering performance and job satisfaction.
  • Suboptimal Career Choices: External validation metrics (e.g., GPA, Leetcode scores) drive career decisions, neglecting intrinsic interests and long-term fulfillment, leading to misalignment between personal goals and professional paths.
  • Skill Atrophy: Overemphasis on measurable achievements (e.g., algorithmic puzzles) undermines development in non-quantifiable skills (e.g., systems thinking, collaboration), creating a lopsided skill set ill-suited to complex, real-world challenges.
  • Market Inefficiencies: Over-investment in signal production (e.g., Leetcode grinding) diverts resources from actual skill development, creating a mismatch between candidate efforts and industry needs, and stifling innovation.

The Physics of the System: A Complex Feedback Network

The system operates as a complex feedback network, where candidate behaviors, selection processes, and information flows interact dynamically. Positive feedback loops (e.g., self-reinforcing perception cycles) amplify perceived requirements, while information asymmetries distort reality. The system’s inherent instability is exacerbated by:

  • Opaque Selection Criteria: Limited visibility into hiring processes prevents candidates from calibrating their efforts effectively, leading to inefficiencies and misaligned expectations.
  • Global Talent Pool Dynamics: International candidates with divergent educational systems compete in unified markets, increasing perceived competition and creating additional barriers for domestic candidates.
  • Cognitive Load Constraints: Candidates must balance technical, soft, and industry-specific skill development, leading to resource allocation inefficiencies and suboptimal outcomes.

Why This Matters: The Stakes of Exceptionalism

The persistence of the exceptionalism narrative in CS carries significant stakes. If unchallenged, it risks:

  • Perpetuating burnout and mental health issues, undermining the well-being of professionals.
  • Discouraging aspiring talent, particularly from underrepresented groups, from entering the field.
  • Narrowing the industry to a homogenous group that fits a narrow definition of success, stifling innovation and diversity.
  • Creating a mismatch between candidate efforts and industry needs, leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal outcomes.

By contrast, recognizing the value of consistent effort, diverse skill sets, and incremental progress can foster a more inclusive, innovative, and sustainable CS ecosystem. This shift requires a reevaluation of selection processes, information dissemination, and societal expectations, but the long-term benefits far outweigh the costs of inaction.

System Reconstruction: Competitive Dynamics in Computer Science (CS)

Mechanisms Driving Competition

The perception of Computer Science (CS) as a domain exclusively for prodigies is perpetuated by several interrelated mechanisms. These mechanisms not only shape the competitive landscape but also contribute to a distorted view of success, fostering unnecessary pressure and undermining the value of diverse skill sets.

  • Hyper-Competitive Selection Processes

Impact: The over-reliance on quantifiable metrics (e.g., Leetcode scores, GPA) narrows the definition of success, marginalizing candidates with diverse skills and fostering over-preparation and anxiety.

Internal Process: Selection systems prioritize measurable achievements as proxies for job performance, creating a feedback loop where candidates feel compelled to excel in these areas at the expense of broader competencies.

Observable Effect: This dynamic leads to a homogenization of the talent pool, where candidates with non-traditional backgrounds or strengths in non-quantifiable areas are systematically disadvantaged.

  • Signal Amplification of 'Prodigy' Candidates

Impact: The disproportionate visibility of high-achieving candidates distorts norms, creating outlier benchmarks that aspirant professionals feel pressured to meet.

Internal Process: Public showcasing of achievements (internships, awards) amplifies the perception that only extraordinary accomplishments are valuable, undervaluing incremental progress and consistent effort.

Observable Effect: Aspirants internalize these elevated standards, leading to a culture of comparison and self-doubt, where even significant achievements are dismissed as insufficient.

  • Self-Reinforcing Perception Cycles

Impact: The observation of high-achieving peers escalates effort and anxiety, creating a collective arms race that inflates requirements and perpetuates overwork.

Internal Process: Candidates raise their standards in response to perceived peer achievements, leading to a self-reinforcing cycle where everyone feels compelled to do more, regardless of personal well-being or long-term sustainability.

Observable Effect: This cycle results in widespread burnout and stress, compromising both individual productivity and the overall health of the industry.

  • Hidden Credentialism

Impact: Unspoken requirements (e.g., network access) act as gatekeepers, exacerbating disparities and discouraging underrepresented groups from entering the field.

Internal Process: Informal criteria, such as access to elite networks or experiences, become de facto prerequisites for success, creating invisible barriers that are difficult to overcome without insider knowledge.

Observable Effect: This mechanism perpetuates systemic inequalities, limiting the diversity of perspectives and innovations that could enrich the field.

  • Asymmetric Information Flow

Impact: Survivor bias in success narratives distorts the perception of competition, leading candidates to overestimate its intensity and discount the importance of resilience and adaptability.

Internal Process: Success stories disproportionately feature high-achievers, omitting the failures, setbacks, and alternative paths that are integral to most careers.

Observable Effect: Candidates internalize a skewed view of what it takes to succeed, often leading to misjudgments about their own capabilities and career trajectories.

System Constraints

The competitive dynamics in CS are further exacerbated by systemic constraints that limit transparency, undervalue critical skills, and create compounding advantages for certain groups.

  • Limited Visibility into Hiring Criteria

Effect: Black-box selection systems force candidates to over-prepare for perceived requirements, leading to inefficiencies and increased stress.

  • Over-Reliance on Quantifiable Metrics

Effect: Non-quantifiable skills (e.g., systems thinking, collaboration) are undervalued, leading to skill atrophy and a workforce ill-equipped to tackle complex, real-world problems.

  • Network Effects in Tech Ecosystems

Effect: Early internships and connections create compounding advantages, widening disparities and limiting opportunities for those without such access.

  • Global Talent Pool Dynamics

Effect: Unified markets with divergent educational systems increase perceived competition, as candidates from different backgrounds are evaluated against a single, often unrealistic standard.

  • Cognitive Load Constraints

Effect: Candidates struggle to balance technical, soft, and industry-specific skill development, leading to suboptimal outcomes and increased risk of burnout.

System Instabilities

The interplay of these mechanisms and constraints gives rise to systemic instabilities that threaten the long-term health and sustainability of the CS industry.

  • Positive Feedback Loops

Mechanism: Candidate behaviors, selection processes, and information flows amplify perceived requirements, leading to escalating standards and unsustainable effort levels.

Effect: This creates a vicious cycle where individuals and organizations are constantly chasing an ever-moving target, with detrimental effects on well-being and productivity.

  • Information Asymmetries

Mechanism: Biased success narratives and opaque selection criteria distort reality, leading to misjudgments about competition intensity and career trajectories.

Effect: Candidates may pursue suboptimal paths or underestimate their own potential, while organizations miss out on talented individuals who do not fit traditional molds.

  • Instability Drivers

Mechanism: Opaque criteria, global talent dynamics, and cognitive load constraints create an environment ripe for instability.

Effect: This leads to widespread burnout, impostor syndrome, and suboptimal career choices, undermining both individual and organizational success.

Observable Failures

The consequences of these dynamics are manifest in several observable failures that highlight the urgent need for systemic change.

  • Burnout: Unsustainable effort levels compromise productivity and well-being, leading to high turnover rates and diminished innovation.
  • Impostor Syndrome: Constant comparison erodes self-confidence, hindering performance and limiting individuals' ability to reach their full potential.
  • Suboptimal Career Choices: External metrics drive decisions, neglecting intrinsic interests and leading to mismatches between individuals and roles.
  • Skill Atrophy: Overemphasis on measurable achievements undermines the development of non-quantifiable skills, creating a workforce that is technically proficient but lacking in critical thinking and creativity.
  • Market Inefficiencies: Over-investment in signal production creates mismatches between efforts and needs, leading to wasted resources and missed opportunities.

Expert Observations

Despite the pervasive narrative of exceptionalism, expert observations reveal alternative pathways to success and challenge the notion that only prodigies can thrive in CS.

  • Non-traditional paths (e.g., career transitions) often lead to success, demonstrating that diverse experiences and skill sets can be valuable assets.
  • There is a weak correlation between algorithmic puzzle performance and actual job performance, suggesting that current selection criteria may be misaligned with real-world demands.
  • Industry demand frequently exceeds "prodigy-level" supply, favoring competent generalists who can adapt to a variety of challenges.
  • Hidden paths (e.g., niche domains) offer lower-competition entry points with comparable outcomes, providing opportunities for those who may not fit the traditional mold.
  • The peer pressure paradox highlights how collectively inflated requirements create artificial barriers, underscoring the need for a more nuanced and inclusive approach to talent development.

Intermediate Conclusions

The analysis reveals that the perception of CS as a domain for prodigies is not only misguided but also detrimental to the field. This narrative fosters unnecessary pressure, undermines the value of consistent effort and diverse skill sets, and risks perpetuating burnout, discouraging aspiring professionals, and narrowing the field to only those who fit a narrow definition of success. By understanding the mechanisms driving this perception, we can begin to challenge and transform the competitive dynamics in CS, fostering a more inclusive, sustainable, and innovative industry.

Analytical Pressure: Why This Matters

The stakes are high. If the current perception persists, it risks stifling innovation and diversity in the industry. By narrowing the field to only those who fit a narrow definition of success, we lose out on the unique perspectives and creative solutions that come from a diverse talent pool. Moreover, the widespread burnout and impostor syndrome resulting from this narrative compromise both individual well-being and organizational productivity. It is imperative that we reevaluate our selection criteria, success narratives, and systemic constraints to create a more equitable and sustainable future for CS.

System Mechanisms and Dynamics in CS Career Perception

The perception of success in Computer Science (CS) is increasingly shaped by a set of interrelated mechanisms that collectively reinforce the notion that only exceptional performance guarantees career advancement. This section dissects these mechanisms, their internal processes, and observable effects, while highlighting their broader implications for individuals and the industry.

Mechanism 1: Hyper-Competitive Selection Processes

  • Impact: The over-reliance on quantifiable metrics (e.g., Leetcode scores, GPA) narrows the definition of success, marginalizing candidates whose strengths lie beyond these metrics.
  • Internal Process: Selection systems prioritize measurable achievements, creating a feedback loop where candidates feel compelled to over-prepare, fueling anxiety and stress.
  • Observable Effect: This homogenizes the talent pool, disadvantages non-traditional candidates, and fosters a short-term focus on test performance rather than long-term skill development. Intermediate Conclusion: By privileging quantifiable metrics, the industry risks losing diverse perspectives and undervaluing critical soft skills.

Mechanism 2: Signal Amplification of 'Prodigy' Candidates

  • Impact: The disproportionate visibility of high-achievers distorts norms, creating an unrealistic benchmark for success.
  • Internal Process: Public showcasing of extraordinary accomplishments amplifies the perception that such achievements are the norm rather than the exception.
  • Observable Effect: Aspirants internalize these elevated standards, fostering unhealthy comparison and self-doubt. Intermediate Conclusion: This mechanism perpetuates a culture of inadequacy, discouraging incremental progress in favor of unattainable ideals.

Mechanism 3: Self-Reinforcing Perception Cycles

  • Impact: The observation of high-achieving peers escalates effort and anxiety, creating a relentless pursuit of validation.
  • Internal Process: Candidates raise their standards in response to perceived peer achievements, often at the expense of well-being.
  • Observable Effect: Widespread burnout and stress compromise productivity and industry health. Intermediate Conclusion: This cycle undermines sustainability, prioritizing short-term gains over long-term career resilience.

Mechanism 4: Hidden Credentialism

  • Impact: Unspoken requirements, such as network access, act as gatekeepers, limiting access to opportunities.
  • Internal Process: Informal criteria become de facto prerequisites, often invisible to outsiders.
  • Observable Effect: This perpetuates systemic inequalities, limits diversity, and discourages underrepresented groups from entering the field. Intermediate Conclusion: Hidden credentialism reinforces privilege, stifling innovation by excluding diverse talent.

Mechanism 5: Asymmetric Information Flow

  • Impact: Survivor bias in success narratives distorts the perception of competition, creating an exaggerated sense of difficulty.
  • Internal Process: Success stories often omit failures and alternative paths, presenting a one-dimensional view of achievement.
  • Observable Effect: Candidates internalize skewed views, leading to misjudgments and overestimation of competition intensity. Intermediate Conclusion: This asymmetry fosters a culture of fear and uncertainty, discouraging risk-taking and exploration.

System Constraints and Instabilities

These mechanisms operate within a broader system constrained by factors that exacerbate their effects. The following constraints highlight the structural challenges that reinforce the perception of exceptionalism in CS careers.

Constraint 1: Limited Visibility into Hiring Criteria

  • Effect: Forces candidates into over-preparation, increases stress, and perpetuates uncertainty. Analytical Pressure: This opacity drives a culture of overwork, as individuals compensate for the lack of clarity with excessive effort.

Constraint 2: Over-Reliance on Quantifiable Metrics

  • Effect: Undervalues non-quantifiable skills, leads to skill atrophy, and neglects holistic development. Analytical Pressure: By prioritizing metrics, the industry risks producing a workforce ill-equipped for complex, real-world challenges.

Constraint 3: Network Effects in Tech Ecosystems

  • Effect: Early access creates compounding advantages, widens disparities, and reinforces privilege. Analytical Pressure: This constraint entrenches inequality, limiting opportunities for those without pre-existing connections.

Constraint 4: Global Talent Pool Dynamics

  • Effect: Unified markets with divergent systems increase perceived competition and create mismatches. Analytical Pressure: This dynamic exacerbates anxiety, as candidates compare themselves to a global standard without understanding contextual differences.

Constraint 5: Cognitive Load Constraints

  • Effect: Balancing skill development leads to suboptimal outcomes, burnout, and compromised well-being. Analytical Pressure: This constraint highlights the unsustainability of current expectations, threatening the long-term health of the workforce.

System Instabilities and Observable Failures

The interplay of these mechanisms and constraints gives rise to systemic instabilities, leading to observable failures that undermine the CS industry’s potential.

Instability 1: Positive Feedback Loops

  • Mechanism: Amplifies perceived requirements, escalates standards, and creates unsustainable effort levels.
  • Observable Failure: Burnout, compromised productivity, and harm to well-being. Connection to Consequences: This instability threatens the industry’s ability to retain talent and innovate sustainably.

Instability 2: Information Asymmetries

  • Mechanism: Biased narratives and opaque criteria distort reality and misguide decision-making.
  • Observable Failure: Suboptimal career choices, missed talent opportunities, and market inefficiencies. Connection to Consequences: This instability perpetuates mismatches between skills and roles, hindering individual and organizational growth.

Instability 3: Instability Drivers

  • Mechanism: Opaque criteria, global dynamics, and cognitive load constraints interact dynamically.
  • Observable Failure: Burnout, impostor syndrome, and suboptimal career choices. Connection to Consequences: This instability fosters a culture of insecurity, undermining confidence and creativity.

Final Analytical Conclusion: The perception that only exceptional performance guarantees success in CS is not only misguided but also detrimental. It fosters unnecessary pressure, undermines the value of consistent effort and diverse skill sets, and risks perpetuating burnout, discouraging aspiring professionals, and narrowing the field. If unaddressed, this perception will stifle innovation, limit diversity, and compromise the industry’s long-term health. Shifting the focus to incremental progress, holistic development, and transparent systems is essential to creating a sustainable and inclusive CS ecosystem.

System Mechanisms in CS Career Dynamics

The competitive landscape of Computer Science (CS) careers is shaped by a complex interplay of mechanisms, constraints, and instabilities that collectively reinforce a misguided perception: only exceptional performance guarantees success. This analysis dissects the technical and psychological processes driving this belief, highlighting its detrimental effects on individuals and the industry at large.

Mechanisms

The following mechanisms underpin the hyper-competitive environment in CS careers, each contributing to the distortion of success metrics and the escalation of pressure on aspirants.

  • Hyper-competitive selection processes:
    • Impact: The over-reliance on quantifiable metrics (e.g., Leetcode scores, GPA) narrows the definition of success, marginalizing candidates who excel in non-quantifiable areas.
    • Internal Process: Selection systems prioritize measurable achievements, creating a feedback loop where candidates feel compelled to over-prepare, fueling anxiety and stress.
    • Observable Effect: This homogenizes the talent pool, disadvantages non-traditional candidates, and fosters a short-term focus on test performance rather than long-term skill development.
  • Signal amplification of 'prodigy' candidates:
    • Impact: The disproportionate visibility of high-achievers distorts norms, creating an unrealistic benchmark for success.
    • Internal Process: Public showcasing of extraordinary achievements amplifies the perception of what is required to succeed, often omitting the effort and failures behind these successes.
    • Observable Effect: Aspirants internalize these elevated standards, fostering a culture of comparison and self-doubt that undermines confidence and mental well-being.
  • Self-reinforcing perception cycles:
    • Impact: Observing high-achieving peers escalates effort and anxiety, as candidates feel pressured to match or exceed perceived standards.
    • Internal Process: Candidates raise their own standards in response to perceived peer achievements, often without a clear understanding of the full context of those achievements.
    • Observable Effect: This leads to widespread burnout and stress, compromising productivity and the overall health of the industry.
  • Hidden credentialism:
    • Impact: Unspoken requirements, such as network access or specific educational backgrounds, act as gatekeepers, limiting opportunities for those outside established circles.
    • Internal Process: Informal criteria become de facto prerequisites, often unacknowledged in formal hiring processes.
    • Observable Effect: This perpetuates systemic inequalities and limits diversity, stifling innovation by excluding valuable perspectives.
  • Asymmetric information flow:
    • Impact: Survivor bias in success narratives distorts the perception of competition, leading candidates to internalize skewed views of what is required to succeed.
    • Internal Process: Success stories often omit failures and alternative paths, presenting a one-dimensional view of achievement.
    • Observable Effect: Candidates make misjudgments about their own paths, often overestimating the importance of certain metrics and underestimating the value of resilience and adaptability.

Constraints

Several constraints exacerbate the pressure on CS aspirants, reinforcing the perception that only exceptional performance is sufficient.

  • Limited visibility into hiring criteria:
    • Effect: The lack of transparency forces candidates into over-preparation, increases stress, and perpetuates uncertainty, as they are unsure what truly matters to employers.
  • Over-reliance on quantifiable metrics:
    • Effect: This undervalues non-quantifiable skills such as problem-solving, teamwork, and creativity, leading to skill atrophy and neglecting holistic development.
  • Network effects in tech ecosystems:
    • Effect: Early access to networks and opportunities creates compounding advantages, widening disparities and reinforcing privilege, further marginalizing those without such access.
  • Global talent pool dynamics:
    • Effect: Unified markets with divergent systems increase perceived competition and create mismatches, as candidates from different regions face varying expectations and standards.
  • Cognitive load constraints:
    • Effect: The need to balance skill development across multiple areas leads to burnout and compromised well-being, as candidates struggle to meet perceived demands.

System Instabilities

The interaction of these mechanisms and constraints creates systemic instabilities that further entrench the perception of exceptionalism as the only path to success.

  • Positive feedback loops:
    • Mechanism: Amplifies perceived requirements, escalating standards and creating an unsustainable cycle of effort.
    • Effect: This leads to unsustainable effort levels, harming well-being and reducing long-term productivity.
  • Information asymmetries:
    • Mechanism: Biased narratives and opaque criteria distort reality, making it difficult for candidates to make informed decisions.
    • Effect: This results in suboptimal career choices and missed talent opportunities, as candidates pursue paths that may not align with their strengths or interests.
  • Instability drivers:
    • Mechanism: The interaction of opaque criteria, global dynamics, and cognitive load constraints creates a volatile environment.
    • Effect: This fosters burnout, impostor syndrome, and suboptimal choices, further narrowing the field to those who can withstand the pressure.

Observable Failures

The persistence of this perception leads to observable failures that undermine both individual well-being and industry health.

  • Burnout: Unsustainable effort compromises productivity and well-being, leading to high turnover and reduced innovation.
  • Impostor syndrome: Constant comparison erodes self-confidence, discouraging talented individuals from pursuing CS careers.
  • Suboptimal career choices: External metrics neglect intrinsic interests, leading to mismatches between individuals and roles, reducing job satisfaction and performance.
  • Skill atrophy: Overemphasis on measurable achievements undermines critical skills such as creativity and adaptability, which are essential for long-term success.
  • Market inefficiencies: Over-investment in signal production (e.g., preparing for specific tests) wastes resources that could be better allocated to skill development and innovation.

Analytical Conclusion

The perception that only exceptional performance guarantees success in CS is not only misguided but also detrimental. It fosters unnecessary pressure, undermines the value of consistent effort and diverse skill sets, and risks perpetuating burnout, discouraging aspiring professionals, and narrowing the field to only those who fit a narrow definition of success. This stifles innovation and diversity, compromising the industry's ability to address complex challenges. By recognizing the mechanisms, constraints, and instabilities driving this perception, stakeholders can work toward creating a more inclusive, sustainable, and innovative CS ecosystem.

title: Character Counter Tools: A Practical Guide for Everyday Writing
description:
Text is part of almost everything we do online. We write messages, descriptions, comments, applications, articles, and posts every day. Many of these tasks have one thing in common: there may be a limit on how much we can write.

A Character Counter can help solve this problem. It provides a quick measurement of text length and can make the editing process much simpler.

Start With Your First Draft

One useful approach is to write naturally before worrying about the exact character count.

Trying to count every character while writing can interrupt your ideas. Instead, create the first version of the content. Once the main message is complete, use a Character Counter to check the length.

This approach separates writing from measurement.

If the content is too long, review it and remove unnecessary information. If it is too short, consider whether additional details would improve the message.

This simple workflow can make writing feel less restrictive.

Check the Important Measurements

Different tasks require different measurements.

Some websites use character limits. Others use word limits. Some forms may provide limits for both.

A good Character Counter tool can show multiple statistics at the same time. This allows users to understand their content more clearly.

For example, you might see the total characters, characters without spaces, words, and paragraphs.

These numbers can help during editing. However, they should support the writing rather than control it. Clear communication should remain the main goal.

Remove Unnecessary Text

After checking the character count, the next step is editing.

Look for repeated ideas and unnecessary phrases. Some sentences can often be shortened without changing their meaning.

For example, a long phrase may be replaced with a simpler expression. Two similar sentences may be combined into one.

The goal is not simply to make the number smaller. The goal is to make the writing more efficient.

A Character Counter gives you the measurement. Your judgement determines what should stay.

Keep Different Platforms in Mind

Content often needs to be adapted for different platforms.

A description that works well on a website may be too long for a smaller text field. A detailed explanation may need to become a short summary.

Checking the character count makes these adaptations easier.

Instead of guessing whether a version will fit, you can measure it directly. This is especially useful when preparing several versions of the same message.

It also creates a repeatable process. Write, measure, edit, and check again.

Make Character Counting Part of Your Workflow

The biggest benefit of a Character Counter is not the number itself. It is the convenience it adds to the writing process.

Once character counting becomes a normal part of editing, text limits become easier to manage.

You can quickly check titles, descriptions, messages, forms, and other content before submitting them.

The process takes only a few seconds, but it can prevent unnecessary rewriting later.

Final Thoughts

A Character Counter is a small tool with many practical uses. It helps writers understand their text and prepare content for different platforms.

The best approach is simple. Write your ideas first, measure the text, edit where necessary, and check the final version.

Whether you are a student, developer, blogger, content creator, or everyday internet user, understanding text length can make online writing easier.

A simple counter may not change what you write, but it can help you deliver the right message within the right space.

title: Attachment downloads should check the record they belong to
description:
Your GET /tickets/:id handler checks that the caller can see the ticket. The files attached to that ticket come from GET /files/:fileId, and that route only checks that someone is logged in.

So anyone holding a file ID can download a screenshot from another customer's support ticket. File IDs end up in notification emails and server logs, and they keep working after a user loses access to the ticket.

What I'd do:

  • Store the parent on the file row (parent_type, parent_id). The download route loads the parent and runs the same check the parent's own endpoint runs.
  • If you hand out signed storage URLs, sign them only after that check passes and keep the expiry short, a few minutes is plenty.
  • Thumbnails, previews and "download all as zip" usually have their own routes. Give them the same check, they are the ones that get missed.
  • Add a test where user A uploads to a ticket and user B from another tenant requests the file ID directly. B should get a 404.

title: Stop writing Excel reports cell by cell - bind data to templates instead (Kotlin/Java)
description:
Still crafting Excel reports cell by cell with POI?

If you've ever built Excel reports in a JVM environment, you know the pain of Apache POI.

// Using Apache POI directly...
val workbook = XSSFWorkbook()
val sheet = workbook.createSheet("Employee Status")
val headerRow = sheet.createRow(0)
headerRow.createCell(0).setCellValue("Name")
headerRow.createCell(1).setCellValue("Position")
headerRow.createCell(2).setCellValue("Salary")

employees.forEachIndexed { index, emp ->
    val row = sheet.createRow(index + 1)
    row.createCell(0).setCellValue(emp.name)
    row.createCell(1).setCellValue(emp.position)
    row.createCell(2).setCellValue(emp.salary.toDouble())
}

// Column widths, styles, formulas, charts... it never ends

One header, one cell, one style at a time... hundreds of lines for a single report.

Add charts, conditional formatting, formulas, and images on top? The code spirals out of control.

TBEG (Template Based Excel Generator) solves this at its root - design the report in Excel, then just bind your data.

What is TBEG?

A JVM library that generates reports by binding data to Excel templates.

The core idea is simple:

  1. A designer (or you) designs the report layout directly in Excel
  2. Place ${variableName} markers where data should go
  3. In your code, just pass the data
  4. TBEG combines template + data to produce the final report 
// Using TBEG - this is all you need to do
val data = mapOf(
    "title" to "Employee Status",
    "employees" to employeeList
)

ExcelGenerator().use { generator ->
    val bytes = generator.generate(template, data)
    File("output.xlsx").writeBytes(bytes)
}

Formatting, charts, formulas, and conditional formatting are all managed in the template. Your code focuses solely on data binding.

Design Philosophy

We don't reinvent what Excel already provides - we use it as-is.

  • Aggregation with Excel's =SUM() formula, averages with =AVERAGE()
  • Conditional highlighting with conditional formatting
  • Visualization with charts

Use the familiar Excel features as they are.

TBEG adds dynamic data binding on top, and automatically adjusts these features to work as intended even when data expands.

At a Glance

Template

Code 

val data = simpleDataProvider {
    value("reportTitle", "Q1 2026 Sales Performance Report")
    value("period", "Jan 2026 ~ Mar 2026")
    value("author", "Yongho Hwang")
    value("reportDate", LocalDate.now().toString())
    image("logo", logoBytes)
    imageUrl("ci", "https://example.com/ci.png")  // URL supported
    items("depts") { deptList.iterator() }
    items("products") { productList.iterator() }
    items("employees") { employeeList.iterator() }
}

ExcelGenerator().use { generator ->
    generator.generateToFile(template, data, outputDir, "quarterly_report")
}

Result

Variable substitution, image insertion, repeat data expansion, automatic cell merge, formula range adjustment, conditional formatting duplication, and chart data reflection - TBEG handles all of this automatically.

Key Features

Feature Description
Template-based generation Generate reports by binding data to Excel templates
Repeat data processing Expand list data into rows/columns with ${repeat(...)} syntax
Variable substitution Bind values to cells, charts, shapes, headers/footers, formula arguments.
Image insertion Insert dynamic images via byte arrays or URLs
Automatic cell merge Auto-merge consecutive cells with the same value in repeat data
Bundle Group multiple elements into a single unit that moves together
Selective field visibility Restrict visibility of specific fields based on conditions. Choose between DELETE or DIM modes
Formula auto-adjustment Automatically update formula ranges (SUM, AVERAGE, etc.) on data expansion
Automatic conditional formatting Automatically apply original conditional formatting to repeated rows
Automatic data validation expansion Automatically apply original data validation (dropdowns, etc.) to repeated rows
Chart/pivot table auto-reflection Automatically reflect expanded data ranges in charts. Pivot table source range auto-adjustment
File encryption Set open password for generated Excel files
Document metadata Set document properties such as title, author, keywords, etc.
Large-scale processing Reliably process over 1 million rows with low CPU utilization
Asynchronous processing Process large data in the background
Lazy loading Memory-efficient data processing via DataProvider
Spring Boot support Easy integration with auto-configuration

Template Syntax Preview

Syntax Description Example
${variableName} Variable substitution ${title}
${object.field} Repeat item field ${emp.name}
${repeat(collection, range, object)} Repeat processing ${repeat(items, A2:C2, item)}
${image(name)} Image insertion ${image(logo)}
${merge(object.field)} Automatic cell merge ${merge(emp.dept)}
${bundle(range)} Bundle ${bundle(A5:H12)}
${hideable(object.field, range, mode)} Selective field visibility ${hideable(emp.salary, C1:C3, DIM)}

Performance

TBEG internally generates data using streaming, producing 1 million rows in about 3.2 seconds while using around 9% of system CPU. Both rendering and post-processing operate in streaming mode, using a constant memory buffer regardless of data size.

Data Size Time CPU Usage
1,000 rows 13ms 25.0%
10,000 rows 47ms 17.4%
30,000 rows 117ms 13.8%
100,000 rows 354ms 11.6%
1,000,000 rows 3,203ms 9.0%

Comparison with Other Libraries (100,000 rows)

Library Time
TBEG 0.35s
JXLS (STREAMING_ON) 0.73s
(ref.) JXLS (STREAMING_OFF) 2.63s

The direct comparison target is JXLS STREAMING_ON, which shares the same output conditions. STREAMING_OFF (full in-memory mode) is a reference figure.

Most Common Use Case: Excel Download API

In practice, TBEG is most frequently used for Excel download features in web applications.

@GetMapping("/api/reports/download")
fun downloadReport(response: HttpServletResponse) {
    val data = reportService.getReportData()
    val template = resourceLoader.getResource("classpath:templates/report.xlsx")

    response.contentType = "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"
    response.setHeader("Content-Disposition", "attachment; filename=report.xlsx")

    excelGenerator.generate(template.inputStream, data)
        .let { response.outputStream.write(it) }
}

Admin page list exports, settlement report downloads, monthly report generation - set up one template and this is all the code you need.

When to Use TBEG

  • ✅ Generating standardized reports/statements
  • ✅ Filling data into Excel forms provided by a designer
  • ✅ Reports requiring complex formatting (conditional formatting, charts)
  • ✅ Processing large datasets with tens to hundreds of thousands of rows
  • ✅ Tables where the number of rows or columns changes with the data
  • ✅ Implementing Excel download APIs in Spring Boot environments
  • ❌ Reading/parsing Excel files (TBEG is generation-only)

Getting Started

Add Dependency 

// build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.jogakdal:tbeg:1.2.5")
}

// Gradle (Groovy DSL)
dependencies {
    implementation 'io.github.jogakdal:tbeg:1.2.5'
}

<!-- Maven -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.jogakdal</groupId>
    <artifactId>tbeg</artifactId>
    <version>1.2.5</version>
</dependency>

The version above is as of this writing. Check the latest version on Maven Central.

Quick Start (Kotlin) 

import io.github.jogakdal.tbeg.ExcelGenerator
import java.io.File

data class Employee(val name: String, val position: String, val salary: Int)

fun main() {
    val data = mapOf(
        "title" to "Employee Status",
        "employees" to listOf(
            Employee("Yongho Hwang", "Director", 8000),
            Employee("Yongho Han", "Manager", 6500)
        )
    )

    ExcelGenerator().use { generator ->
        val template = File("template.xlsx").inputStream()
        val bytes = generator.generate(template, data)
        File("output.xlsx").writeBytes(bytes)
    }
}

Quick Start (Java) 

import io.github.jogakdal.tbeg.ExcelGenerator;
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var data = Map.<String, Object>of(
            "title", "Employee Status",
            "employees", List.of(
                Map.of("name", "Yongho Hwang", "position", "Director", "salary", 8000),
                Map.of("name", "Yongho Han", "position", "Manager", "salary", 6500)
            )
        );

        try (var generator = new ExcelGenerator()) {
            byte[] bytes = generator.generate(
                new FileInputStream("template.xlsx"), data);
            Files.write(Path.of("output.xlsx"), bytes);
        }
    }
}

Learn More

This is the first post in the TBEG series. In the next post, we'll walk through creating a template and binding data step by step.

  • Maven Central: tbeg
