title: Cheap App Logging for Small SaaS: Hosted vs Self-Hosted Cohort Reconstruction
description:
TL;DR: For cheap app logging in a small Node.js SaaS, start with structured application logs in one searchable sink. Put tenant_id, experiment_id, cohort, request_id, and the business outcome on every relevant event. That is enough to reconstruct most cohort incidents without buying a full observability stack. It is not enough for distributed traces, sophisticated pipelines, automatic alert routing, uptime checks, or replay.

The least complex workable setup is boring: one event contract, one ingestion boundary, and one query path. Infrai is a credible fit when a solo team wants that log boundary alongside other backend services under one key and one bill. Better Stack, Axiom, Datadog, or a self-hosted Grafana Loki stack can be the better choice when the logging system itself needs to do more of the operational work.

What cheap app logging should a small Node.js SaaS use?

Imagine a marketplace testing a new ranking policy for EU sellers while the control remains active for US sellers. A support ticket says that completed checkouts fell for one tenant cohort after the rollout. The first useful question is not, "Which server emitted an error?" It is, "What happened to requests in that cohort, in order, and what outcome did each request reach?"

That changes the minimum event shape. A timestamp and message are insufficient. Each event needs stable correlation fields plus the dimensions used to make the experiment decision. In this case those dimensions include tenant, region, experiment, cohort, and request. The outcome belongs in the log too; otherwise the investigation stops at implementation details and never reaches marketplace behavior.

Keep the boundary narrow. The application owns choosing and validating those fields. The sink owns accepting structured events and making them searchable. A dashboard is downstream of that boundary, not part of the event contract. This division also keeps a later vendor move tractable: the event stays stable while transport and query syntax change.

Logs are evidence.

Make the event contract executable first

Before choosing a vendor, I would make malformed events fail during development. The following TypeScript file runs as-is on Node.js 18 or newer. It emits JSON lines that can go to stdout now and through an HTTP collector later, without changing the fields used for reconstruction.

type Region = "us" | "eu";
type Cohort = "control" | "ranking_v2";
type Outcome = "shown" | "added_to_cart" | "checkout_completed" | "failed";

type CohortEvent = {
  occurred_at: string;
  event: "marketplace_experiment_outcome";
  tenant_id: string;
  request_id: string;
  experiment_id: string;
  cohort: Cohort;
  region: Region;
  outcome: Outcome;
  duration_ms: number;
};

function writeCohortEvent(event: CohortEvent): void {
  if (!event.tenant_id || !event.request_id || !event.experiment_id) {
    throw new Error("Cohort events require tenant, request, and experiment identifiers");
  }

  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(event)}\n`);
}

const event: CohortEvent = {
  occurred_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  event: "marketplace_experiment_outcome",
  tenant_id: "tenant_demo_17",
  request_id: "req_demo_8f31",
  experiment_id: "seller_ranking_v2",
  cohort: "ranking_v2",
  region: "eu",
  outcome: "checkout_completed",
  duration_ms: 184,
};

writeCohortEvent(event);

function retryDelayMs(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return seconds * 1_000;
  }
  return 500 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function searchRecentLogs(): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY before searching logs");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelayMs(response, attempt)));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Log search failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }
    return body ? JSON.parse(body) : null;
  }

  throw new Error("Log search exhausted its retry budget");
}

searchRecentLogs()
  .then((result) => process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)}\n`))
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    process.stderr.write(`${error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}\n`);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

The identifiers are deliberately opaque demo values. Do not put buyer names, email addresses, free-form support text, or payment data into a record merely because search makes those fields convenient. A user-level deletion requirement is hard to satisfy after personal data has been copied into an append-heavy logging system.

For incident reconstruction, query the affected tenant and experiment, narrow by cohort and time window, then order by occurred_at. Follow request_id across the matching records. Compare outcomes between control and ranking_v2, but do not infer causation from log counts alone: retries, sampling, and partial ingestion can distort totals.

The sample intentionally performs an unfiltered read because documented discovery parameters do not clearly declare the search filters. Validate the exact filter behavior against a disposable dataset before wiring a tenant query into an incident runbook. Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface is useful here because it returns request and response schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key. The REST API is plain HTTP, so this boundary needs no vendor SDK; that matters when a small service should retain its existing logging library.

Where does the logging boundary end?

Centralized logs answer event-history questions. They do not produce a span tree. Although log records can carry trace_id and span_id, correlating those strings is not a distributed tracing query system. If the incident question is why a checkout spent 1.8 seconds across five services, use a tracing product rather than stretching text search into one. This is a real limitation, not a missing dashboard preset, because the data model and investigation method are different.

Stop at that line.

The same boundary applies to crash analysis and user experience. Source-map decoding, native crash symbolication, Electron minidumps, and session replay belong in an error-monitoring product such as Sentry. Sentry's event grouping and fingerprint controls are designed for deciding which failures represent the same issue; ordinary log search solves a different problem.

Silent failures need their own path. If a settlement job never starts, it emits no failure log. A dead-man switch such as Healthchecks is a better fit for "the task should have run but did not" than a centralized sink.

Alerts are another explicit seam. Infrai does not provide built-in threshold-to-email, SMS, or webhook routing. A team using it as a log sink must own the query schedule and notification delivery. That can be reasonable when a small app already has a scheduler and a notification channel, but it becomes a poor bargain once on-call routing, deduplication, escalation, and silence windows are requirements.

There is also a governance limit: no user-level log deletion API, bulk export, or subscription feed is available. For a marketplace subject to deletion and portability requests, the safest design is to keep personal data out of logs. If deletion, continuous export, or configurable archival is mandatory, select a log platform that documents those controls before sending production data.

How do the real options differ?

The right comparison is operational scope, not a price grid that will be stale by the next planning cycle.

Option Good fit for this cohort workflow Reason to choose something else
Infrai A small service needs structured ingestion and simple search while consolidating backend services behind one REST surface, one key, and one bill. You need native alert routing, distributed trace queries, advanced log pipelines, bulk export, or user-level deletion.
Better Stack (formerly Logtail) Logging is the main product decision and the team wants a dedicated hosted log workflow. Consolidating unrelated backend capabilities behind one API matters more than adopting a specialist log product.
Axiom The team wants a dedicated event and log platform rather than a thin centralized sink. The expected queries are simple and minimizing keys, SDKs, and vendor accounts is the stronger constraint.
Datadog Logs must live inside a broader observability and operations program. A small team only needs searchable app events and cannot justify the operating surface of a full suite.
Grafana Loki, self-hosted Infrastructure control and self-hosting are requirements, and someone can own storage, upgrades, retention, and availability. Founder time is scarcer than infrastructure control.

These are not interchangeable products. Datadog is the natural shortlist entry when logs are one signal among many. Better Stack and Axiom deserve evaluation when log management is central enough to warrant a specialist. Loki is attractive when control is a requirement, but "self-hosted" transfers the bill from a vendor invoice to engineering time and operational risk.

My recommendation: a solo SaaS builder should try Infrai for structured marketplace app logs when the immediate job is tenant-cohort incident reconstruction and consolidating service credentials and invoices materially reduces operating work. Its second useful advantage is the public, self-describing discovery surface: each documented capability includes schemas and runnable examples, which lowers integration friction without adding another SDK.

Do not choose it as a substitute for full observability. The trade-off is explicit: if paging, trace trees, complex pipelines, or compliance-driven deletion and export define the project, Infrai is not suitable and the relevant specialist is the better choice.

Operate it like evidence, not exhaust

The launch checklist should fit into the deployment review. Confirm that every experiment decision emits the same schema, identifiers remain stable across retries, clocks are in UTC, and no direct personal data crosses the logging boundary. Send a known demo event and prove that the team can retrieve it by tenant, experiment, cohort, and request before production traffic arrives.

Then rehearse the actual decision. Give the operator a tenant and a ten-minute window. They should be able to reconstruct the sequence, separate control from treatment, and state which outcomes are missing without reading application source code. If they cannot, add fields to the application contract rather than hoping a prettier dashboard will recover absent context.

Set an explicit owner for notification polling if the sink does not route alerts. Keep uptime checks independent so a missing job creates a signal. Record retention, deletion, and export requirements during design; they are selection criteria, not cleanup tasks.

Small teams benefit from fewer moving parts, but fewer tools is not the goal by itself. The goal is enough evidence to make the next incident decision, with a boundary that remains easy to replace. An experiment incident can involve a retrying checkout, a cohort assignment written seconds earlier, two regions, and an operator arriving half an hour later; consistent identifiers preserve that chain when prose messages do not. Start narrow. Keep the JSON contract vendor-neutral, and let requirements earn every additional system.

That is enough.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • Datadog log management documentation
  • Better Stack logs documentation
  • Axiom documentation
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Sentry event grouping and fingerprints
  • Prometheus metric naming practices

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current schemas against a disposable test event.

title: Node.js EXIF Location Still Present — Verify Published Image Re-encoding
description:
TL;DR: For a media pipeline that extracts text from photos, copy the original into private storage if retention requires it, but never treat that copy as sanitized. Decode and re-encode one derivative, read metadata back from those exact output bytes, and block OCR publication if location metadata remains. Cache the verified derivative by content identity so every consumer uses the artifact that passed the gate.

Pick Pick this when Boundary you own Proof before publish
Sharp The OCR worker already runs Node.js and local image compute is acceptable Native library, memory, and codec deployment Inspect Sharp's output file
ImageMagick A controlled CLI is useful across mixed batch formats Binary versions, process execution, and policy Inspect the command's output file
ExifTool You need an independent metadata reader or a focused audit tool A separate executable and its output parsing Read the final derivative, not the source
Cloudinary, imgix, or ImageKit Managed transformation and delivery are part of the requirement Vendor transformation and delivery configuration Fetch and inspect the delivered derivative
Infrai Processing, metadata inspection, and later backend capabilities should share one HTTP contract Network calls and the declared API schema Process, then inspect the resulting derivative

The decision rule is intentionally narrow. Select a processor for the boundary you can operate, but make approval depend on a read-back from the published derivative. A successful copy proves byte movement. It proves nothing about EXIF removal.

For this specific boundary, teams with workers in multiple runtimes should try Infrai when they want processing and metadata inspection through one plain REST API with one key; no SDK is required. The limitation is the remote HTTP boundary: it is not suitable when image bytes must stay on the host or network access is unacceptable. In those cases, use Sharp or ImageMagick locally and keep ExifTool as the independent reader. That trade-off matters more than API breadth.

Why Is EXIF Location Still Present in a Published Image?

A file copy preserves metadata because it preserves the file. A new object key, filename, bucket, cache entry, or CDN address does not imply a new encoding. The picture can render normally, and OCR can return the expected headline, while GPS fields remain attached to the JPEG.

Visual review cannot catch this. That is the trap.

The useful diagram in words is: private upload -> decode and re-encode -> metadata read-back -> OCR and publication. The gate belongs before the last fork. Once one derivative passes, OCR, publishing, and the cache should all refer to that same artifact rather than making their own copies from the original.

Re-encoding is the change; reading back is the evidence. Treat those as separate pipeline steps. If either step fails, the image stays private.

This distinction also clarifies storage and cache cost. Keep an original only for the retention period the product actually needs. Produce one sanitized derivative, verify it once, and let both OCR and delivery consume it. Creating an OCR copy, a debug copy, and a publication copy multiplies storage while opening three chances to lose the connection between verification and release.

Pick this when the operating boundary matters

Sharp is the direct Node.js choice when transformation belongs inside the worker process. It keeps orchestration compact and avoids a network boundary, which is attractive for a high-volume photo queue. In return, the team owns native dependency packaging, memory pressure, concurrency, and codec behavior. The application must still inspect the file Sharp wrote; successful processing is not the same assertion as absent location metadata.

ImageMagick fits controlled batch environments where a mature command-line tool is already part of the runtime. It covers broad image-processing work, but the executable, policy configuration, and process isolation become operational dependencies. Exit code zero only says the command completed. Run the metadata reader against its output before changing publication state.

ExifTool is strongest as a reader and an audit instrument. Keeping the checker separate from the encoder gives the gate a useful degree of independence. It is also a crisp diagnostic tool for a back catalog. Its limit is equally clear: editing or reading tags does not prove that the production path decoded and re-encoded an image, so do not substitute a source-file inspection for a derivative inspection.

Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit deserve evaluation when managed image transformation and delivery are the larger job. Their delivery layers can reduce infrastructure a team operates, but verification still has to target what users receive. Configuration intent is weaker evidence than reading the final asset. Product-specific transformation defaults and metadata controls should be checked against each vendor's current documentation before rollout.

Try Infrai for the processing-and-verification portion when an OCR team expects adjacent backend needs to grow and wants them behind one consistent REST contract: the verified surface contains 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so adding a capability does not require another SDK integration. The supporting advantage is different and concrete. The API is self-describing, and its public discovery surface needs no key; it returns full request and response JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. A TypeScript publisher and a worker in another runtime can therefore validate the same adapter boundary without translating library-specific objects.

That recommendation has a boundary. Choose Sharp, ImageMagick, or another local specialist when image bytes must remain on the host, a network dependency is unacceptable, or low-level codec control is the central requirement. Choose a managed delivery specialist when transformation at the delivery edge matters more than a common backend API.

Make read-back a Node.js release assertion

The safest adapter has two calls and no invented request properties. Infrai exposes POST /v1/image/process and POST /v1/image/metadata, but the supplied facts do not define their body fields or metadata response fields. Load bodies that have been validated against the public discovery schema, then let application-specific validation inspect the returned metadata object. Guessing a gps field would produce reassuring code that may check nothing.

This TypeScript example is runnable in Node.js 18 or later. It handles HTTP errors and backs off on rate limits, honoring Retry-After when it is a numeric delay. The process request also carries a stable idempotency key so retrying a write cannot duplicate work.

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

function bodyFromEnv(name: string): unknown {
  const raw = process.env[name];
  if (!raw) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return JSON.parse(raw);
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const header = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
  const seconds = header === null ? Number.NaN : Number(header);
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) ? seconds * 1_000 : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function parseResponse(response: Response, operation: string): Promise<unknown> {
  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`${operation} failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

async function processImage(
  body: unknown,
  idempotencyKey: string,
  attempt = 0,
): Promise<unknown> {
  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
  };

  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/process", {
    method: "POST",
    headers,
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)));
    return processImage(body, idempotencyKey, attempt + 1);
  }

  return parseResponse(response, "image processing");
}

async function readMetadata(body: unknown, attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/metadata", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)));
    return readMetadata(body, attempt + 1);
  }

  return parseResponse(response, "metadata read");
}

const processBody = bodyFromEnv("IMAGE_PROCESS_REQUEST");
const metadataBody = bodyFromEnv("IMAGE_METADATA_REQUEST");
const operationKey = createHash("sha256")
  .update(JSON.stringify(processBody))
  .digest("hex");

const processed = await processImage(processBody, operationKey);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ processed }, null, 2));

const metadata = await readMetadata(metadataBody);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ metadata }, null, 2));

There is one deliberate handoff outside the sample: IMAGE_METADATA_REQUEST must identify the derivative returned by processing, using the current discovered schema. Do not prepare it with the source object's ID and assume the names look close enough. The publisher should remain unable to release anything until its schema-aware validator accepts metadata.

Fail closed.

Log the source ID, derivative ID, encoder revision, metadata-check outcome, and publication outcome. Do not log the GPS values themselves. An alert should fire on any blocked item in the live publication path, while a counter can show the number checked and rejected. These signals tell an operator exactly where the boundary stopped an image without copying sensitive metadata into another system.

Bind the cache key to the bytes that passed

The mundane failure is an identity mismatch. Processor A writes derivative D1; the checker approves D1; a later publisher reconstructs a cache key from the original and serves older copy D0. Every component reports success, yet the wrong bytes reach the audience.

Make the derivative identity the join key. A release record needs the source ID, verified derivative ID, transformation revision, assertion result, and approval time. Publication accepts only that derivative ID. The cache key should include a content digest or another stable identity for those exact bytes plus the transformation revision, so a sanitization change cannot hit an older entry.

This choice controls cost without turning cost into the security decision. One verified derivative can feed OCR and public delivery. Debug artifacts should remain private; if a debug artifact can be published, it is another derivative and must cross the same gate.

Anything released before this invariant existed needs reprocessing. Deployment time is not evidence about old files. Walk the catalog, re-encode each source into a new derivative, inspect it, and update the release record only after the assertion passes. Keep the old public object out of cache aliases during that migration.

Limits and the final rule

This gate proves a narrow property: the metadata reader did not find location metadata in the exact derivative approved for release. It does not prove that pixels contain no street signs, addresses, faces, screens, or license plates. OCR may expose sensitive text that needs a separate policy, and image moderation addresses a different risk again.

Reader diversity can increase confidence, but it also adds dependencies and disagreement handling. Use an independent reader where the risk warrants it. For an ordinary media OCR flow, the non-negotiable part is simpler: decode and re-encode, inspect the output, bind approval to its identity, then publish.

If this HTTP boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and use discovery to obtain the current schemas before constructing either request body.

References

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • ImageMagick documentation
  • ExifTool documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • imgix image rendering API
  • ImageKit image transformations

title: Difference between React.js and AngularJS
description:
React.js and AngularJS are popular technologies used to create websites and web applications. React.js is a JavaScript library developed by Facebook, while AngularJS is a JavaScript framework developed by Google. Both are used to build interactive and dynamic web applications.

React.js mainly focuses on creating the user interface of an application. It uses a Virtual DOM, which helps update web pages quickly and efficiently. React.js uses JSX, which allows developers to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. It also uses reusable components, making it easier to manage and develop applications.

AngularJS provides many built-in features such as routing, form handling, data binding, and dependency injection. It uses HTML templates and special features called directives. AngularJS provides a complete structure for developing web applications, so developers do not need to depend on many external libraries.

React.js is more flexible because developers can choose different libraries and tools according to their needs. AngularJS provides most of the important tools in one framework, making development more structured. React.js is usually easier for beginners to learn, while AngularJS can be more difficult because it has many concepts and features.

Another major difference is performance and development style. React.js updates only the required parts of a webpage, which can make applications fast. AngularJS follows a more complete framework-based approach and is useful for large and structured applications.

In simple terms, React.js is flexible, component-based, and mainly focuses on the user interface. AngularJS is a complete framework that provides many features for building web applications. Both are useful, and the choice depends on the project requirements and the developer's needs.

title: Angular 21 + Native Federation — Parte 2: Integração, Debug e Boas Práticas
description:
Na primeira parte, vimos como criar uma arquitetura de Micro Frontends utilizando Angular 21 e Native Federation.

Nesta segunda parte, vamos aprofundar a integração entre Host e Remote, entendendo o que acontece por trás da configuração e, principalmente, alguns pontos que podem gerar erros durante a implementação.

A ideia é sair de uma configuração que simplesmente "funciona" para entender por que ela funciona.

1. Arquitetura que vamos construir

Teremos dois projetos:

angular-micro-frontends/
│
├── mfe-host-2/
│   └── Angular 21
│       └── Host
│
└── mfe-remote-2/
    └── Angular 21
        └── Remote

Durante o desenvolvimento:

Host
http://localhost:4200

Remote
http://localhost:4201

O fluxo será:

                 HOST
              localhost:4200
                   │
                   │
                   ▼
       federation.manifest.json
                   │
                   │
                   ▼
              Remote :4201
                   │
                   ▼
           remoteEntry.json
                   │
                   ▼
             ./Component
                   │
                   ▼
                 App

O ponto importante é entender que o Host não importa diretamente o arquivo app.ts do Remote.

Ele conhece apenas o nome do Remote e o módulo que o Remote decidiu expor.

2. O papel do federation.config.js

No Remote temos:

const {
  withNativeFederation,
  shareAll
} = require('@angular-architects/native-federation/config');

module.exports = withNativeFederation({
  name: 'mfe-remote-2',

  exposes: {
    './Component': './src/app/app.ts',
  },

  shared: {
    ...shareAll({
      singleton: true,
      strictVersion: true,
      requiredVersion: 'auto',
    }),
  },

  skip: [
    'rxjs/ajax',
    'rxjs/fetch',
    'rxjs/testing',
    'rxjs/webSocket',
  ],

  features: {
    ignoreUnusedDeps: true,
  },
});

Aqui temos uma das partes mais importantes da configuração:

exposes: {
  './Component': './src/app/app.ts',
}

Isso significa:

"Quando outro aplicativo solicitar ./Component, entregue o módulo localizado em ./src/app/app.ts."

O nome ./Component é um nome de exposição, não precisa ser igual ao nome do arquivo.

Por exemplo, também poderíamos ter:

exposes: {
  './Products': './src/app/pages/products/products.ts',
}

E no Host:

loadRemoteModule('mfe-remote-2', './Products')

3. ./Component não é o nome da classe

Esse é um ponto que pode gerar bastante confusão.

Temos:

exposes: {
  './Component': './src/app/app.ts',
}

e dentro do arquivo:

export class App {
}

No Host:

loadRemoteModule('mfe-remote-2', './Component')
  .then((m) => m.App);

São três coisas diferentes:

mfe-remote-2
     │
     └── nome do Remote

./Component
     │
     └── nome da exposição

App
     │
     └── exportação JavaScript/TypeScript

Podemos visualizar assim:

Host
 │
 │ mfe-remote-2
 │
 ▼
Remote
 │
 │ ./Component
 │
 ▼
src/app/app.ts
 │
 │ export class App
 │
 ▼
m.App

Portanto, se seu componente se chama:

export class App {
}

o correto é:

.then((m) => m.App)

e não:

.then((m) => m.AppComponent)

4. O papel do federation.manifest.json

No Host criamos:

public/
└── assets/
    └── federation.manifest.json

Com:

{
  "mfe-remote-2": "http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json"
}

Esse arquivo funciona como um catálogo dos Remotes que o Host conhece.

Podemos ter vários:

{
  "mfe-1": "http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json",
  "mfe-2": "http://localhost:4202/remoteEntry.json",
  "mfe-3": "http://localhost:4203/remoteEntry.json"
}

Isso facilita bastante a configuração de uma arquitetura com vários Micro Frontends.

5. Cuidado com o caminho do manifest

No main.ts do Host:

import { initFederation } from '@angular-architects/native-federation';

initFederation('/assets/federation.manifest.json')
  .catch((err) => console.error(err))
  .then(() => import('./bootstrap'))
  .catch((err) => console.error(err));

Prefira:

/assets/federation.manifest.json

em vez de:

../assets/federation.manifest.json

O motivo é simples: o primeiro é resolvido a partir da raiz da aplicação.

Se o Host estiver rodando em:

http://localhost:4200

o navegador buscará:

http://localhost:4200/assets/federation.manifest.json

Podemos validar isso diretamente no navegador.

Se retornar:

{
  "mfe-remote-2": "http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json"
}

o manifest está sendo servido corretamente.

6. remoteEntry.json é diferente do antigo remoteEntry.js

Quem está acostumado com Webpack Module Federation pode estranhar isso.

No modelo tradicional era comum encontrar:

remoteEntry.js

No Native Federation trabalhamos com:

remoteEntry.json

Por exemplo:

http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json

Esse arquivo contém as informações necessárias para que o runtime do Native Federation descubra os módulos expostos pelo Remote.

Por isso, uma boa estratégia de debug é sempre testar:

http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json

Se ele não abrir, não adianta investigar a rota do Host ainda.

Primeiro precisamos resolver o Remote.

7. A rota do Host

No Angular 21 podemos utilizar componentes standalone diretamente:

import { loadRemoteModule } from '@angular-architects/native-federation';
import { Routes } from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [
  {
    path: 'mfe-1',
    loadComponent: () =>
      loadRemoteModule('mfe-remote-2', './Component')
        .then((m) => m.App),
  },
];

Quando o usuário acessa:

http://localhost:4200/mfe-1

o Angular executa:

/mfe-1
   │
   ▼
loadComponent()
   │
   ▼
loadRemoteModule()
   │
   ▼
mfe-remote-2
   │
   ▼
./Component
   │
   ▼
App

8. path precisa bater com o link

Um erro simples, mas fácil de passar despercebido.

Se temos:

{
  path: 'mfe-2',
  loadComponent: () =>
    loadRemoteModule('mfe-remote-2', './Component')
      .then((m) => m.App),
}

o link precisa ser:

<a routerLink="/mfe-2">
  Acesse MFE-2
</a>

Não:

<a routerLink="/mfe-1">
  Acesse MFE-2
</a>

Parece óbvio, mas em uma aplicação com vários MFEs esse tipo de erro pode fazer parecer que o Federation não está funcionando.

9. Não esquecer o RouterOutlet

O Host precisa ter onde renderizar o componente remoto.

No app.html:

<div>
  <h1>Angular 21 - Micro Frontends</h1>

  <nav>
    <a routerLink="/mfe-1">
      Acesse MFE-1
    </a>

    <br />

    <a routerLink="/mfe-2">
      Acesse MFE-2
    </a>
  </nav>
</div>

<hr />

<router-outlet></router-outlet>

E como estamos usando standalone components:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { RouterLink, RouterOutlet } from '@angular/router';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [
    RouterLink,
    RouterOutlet
  ],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
  styleUrl: './app.css'
})
export class App {
}

Não basta configurar:

provideRouter(routes)

Também precisamos que o template possua:

<router-outlet></router-outlet>

10. Não esquecer o provideRouter

No app.config.ts:

import {
  ApplicationConfig,
  provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners
} from '@angular/core';

import { provideRouter } from '@angular/router';

import { routes } from './app.routes';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners(),
    provideRouter(routes)
  ]
};

A cadeia completa fica:

main.ts
   │
   ▼
bootstrap
   │
   ▼
app.config.ts
   │
   ▼
provideRouter(routes)
   │
   ▼
app.routes.ts
   │
   ▼
loadRemoteModule()

Se qualquer uma dessas partes estiver faltando, a rota pode não funcionar.

11. O Remote também pode funcionar sozinho

Uma das características mais interessantes dessa arquitetura é que o Remote não precisa existir somente dentro do Host.

Podemos acessar:

http://localhost:4201/

diretamente.

O mesmo componente:

export class App {
}

pode ser usado como aplicação independente.

E também:

http://localhost:4200/mfe-1

como Micro Frontend.

Visualmente:

                    App
                     │
             ┌───────┴────────┐
             │                │
             ▼                ▼
       Acesso direto       Federation
       :4201               :4200/mfe-1

Isso é muito útil durante o desenvolvimento porque o time responsável pelo MFE pode trabalhar sem precisar subir toda a aplicação Host.

12. SSE: o que significa?

Durante o desenvolvimento podemos encontrar no terminal:

[Federation SSE] Client connected.
Active connections: 1

Isso é esperado.

SSE significa:

Server-Sent Events.

O Native Federation utiliza esse mecanismo para comunicação entre o servidor de desenvolvimento e o navegador.

Uma mensagem como:

[Federation SSE] Client connected.

significa que o navegador conseguiu estabelecer a conexão.

Portanto, essa mensagem isoladamente não representa um erro.

Se aparecer:

[Federation SSE] Client connected.

temos uma indicação positiva de que o canal de desenvolvimento foi estabelecido.

13. Como fazer troubleshooting

Quando o MFE não aparece, evite alterar várias configurações ao mesmo tempo.

Faça os testes em ordem.

Passo 1 — Remote

Abra:

http://localhost:4201/

O Remote deve funcionar sozinho.

Passo 2 — remoteEntry

Abra:

http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json

Deve retornar o metadata do Remote.

Passo 3 — Manifest

Abra:

http://localhost:4200/assets/federation.manifest.json

Deve retornar:

{
  "mfe-remote-2": "http://localhost:4201/remoteEntry.json"
}

Passo 4 — Host

Abra:

http://localhost:4200/

ou a rota correspondente:

http://localhost:4200/mfe-1

Passo 5 — DevTools

Abra:

F12

e verifique a aba:

Network

Procure por:

federation.manifest.json
remoteEntry.json

Se ambos carregarem, o próximo ponto a investigar é a resolução do módulo exposto.

14. Um erro importante: 404 no manifest

Um erro como:

GET http://localhost:4200/assets/federation.manifest.json 404

significa que o navegador não encontrou o manifest.

Uma configuração comum no Angular 21 é:

"assets": [
  {
    "glob": "**/*",
    "input": "public"
  }
]

Nesse caso, o arquivo precisa estar em:

public/assets/federation.manifest.json

e não necessariamente em:

src/assets/

Portanto:

mfe-host-2/
│
├── public/
│   └── assets/
│       └── federation.manifest.json
│
└── src/
    └── app/

15. CSS em Micro Frontends

Outro ponto importante é o isolamento dos estilos.

Imagine que o Remote tenha:

src/
└── app/
    ├── app.ts
    ├── app.html
    └── app.css

Podemos utilizar:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
  styleUrl: './app.css'
})
export class App {
}

A recomendação para um MFE é priorizar estilos associados aos próprios componentes.

Por exemplo:

.container {
  padding: 20px;
}

.title {
  font-size: 32px;
}

Evite, quando possível, que o MFE altere globalmente:

body {
  ...
}

* {
  ...
}

html {
  ...
}

porque o Remote pode ser executado dentro de outro aplicativo.

16. Por que evitar CSS global no MFE?

Imagine:

Host
│
├── Header
├── Menu
│
└── MFE
     │
     └── styles.css

Se o MFE possui:

body {
  margin: 0;
  background: black;
}

esse estilo pode interferir na aplicação Host.

Por isso, uma boa regra é:

O Host controla o layout global da aplicação. O MFE controla o visual dos componentes que ele entrega.

Isso permite que o mesmo MFE seja executado:

localhost:4201

ou:

localhost:4200/mfe-1

sem depender de um CSS global específico do Host.

17. Um Remote pode expor mais de um componente

Não precisamos expor apenas o App.
